title: We’ve Received Your Feedback. Now What?
subtitle: A work schedule, a piano practice log and a course application: how to tell whether something was actually taken into account.
intro: In the last box on the scheduling feedback form, Lin writes that she needs to pick up her child on Wednesday evenings and would prefer an early shift whenever possible. Worried that this might not be clear enough, she adds the time.
She presses Submit. A message appears: We’ve received your feedback.
A few days later, the new schedule comes out. She is still on the late shift on Wednesday. When she asks about it, the answer is: We’ve recorded all your comments.

It is easy to jump to a conclusion: they simply don’t care about her. Someone else might say, “They asked for everyone’s preferences. They can’t please everybody.” There’s feeling behind both responses. Neither quite answers the question she wants to ask.
What actually happened to the thing I told you?

The everyday situations below are made-up examples, not findings from an investigation into a particular workplace. Before deciding who is right or wrong, let’s follow that piece of feedback a little further.

sections.heading: 1. Who opened the form?
paragraphs: Suppose the shop collected this information so it could assign shifts people could actually work and reduce last-minute swaps. The form listed each person’s available hours and included a box for comments.

But when the person making the schedule received the file, they copied only the names and existing shifts into a new spreadsheet. They never opened the comments, never used them to check availability, and had no colleague responsible for bringing individual constraints into the scheduling discussion. The file was safely stored. Not one comment was lost.

In this scenario, Lin’s constraint never entered the scheduling process. We know that not because she ended up on the late shift, but because we found where her information stopped. It remained in the file. The work that followed did not use it.
It is like writing “take your keys” on a sticky note, then leaving the note in a drawer. However clearly you wrote it, it played no part in your check before leaving the house.

But we also need to be clear about which job we are checking. If the task was simply to archive everyone’s submissions exactly as written, keeping them safely might have completed that task. An archivist has not failed to archive something just because they have no authority to change a shift.

Whether the comments were properly archived and whether the schedule took this constraint into account are two different questions. “We’ve recorded everything” can obscure the difference by presenting an answer to the first as an answer to the second.

sections.heading: 2. What was this supposed to do?
paragraphs: Whether a form is useful depends first on what it is for.

If the aim is to assign shifts people can work, Lin’s availability on Wednesday evening matters. Whether she can work that shift or cannot work it gives the scheduler different arrangements to consider. Whether she prefers blue or green usually makes no difference to this task. Not asking for her favourite colour is not, by itself, an omission.

There are two plain questions here. First: if this particular fact were different, would pursuing the same purpose call for doing something differently? Second: did that fact reach a part of the process where, under the relevant conditions, it could actually affect how the matter was handled?

The first question asks whether the information is relevant. The second asks whether it was taken into the process. We cannot assume a detail matters just because nobody asked about it. Nor can we assume it was put to use just because the form had a box for it.

We cannot casually rewrite the purpose after seeing the outcome, either. If the shop said it was collecting information to make workable schedules, we cannot decide that it was “only collecting forms all along” merely because the schedule stayed the same. Conversely, if the stated task really was just to archive people’s exact words, we cannot quietly expand it into solving everyone’s difficulties. We need to look at how the task was described at the time, how it connected to the work that followed, and what was actually being done.

If the explanation and the practice do not match, lay them side by side: what the shop undertook to do, and what the available evidence shows it doing. Don’t flatten the difference with “It all amounts to the same thing.”

sections.heading: 3. Forty minutes won’t tell you which bar went wrong
paragraphs: This way of asking questions is not just for checking on organisations. We can use it to look at our own small habits.
Suppose you practise the piano and record just one number each day: how many minutes you played. Forty on Monday. Forty on Tuesday. Forty again on Wednesday. The neat rows are reassuring.

If all you want to check is whether you practised for at least forty minutes each day, and the times are accurate, the log can already answer your question. It does not need to record every note to do that limited job.

But if you want to use it to decide which bars to focus on tomorrow, forty minutes is not enough. One day you keep getting stuck at the beginning; another day you keep making mistakes at the end. Both entries show the same number. Yet the two situations give you different reasons for where to spend tomorrow’s practice time.

Suppose you have no recording, no marks on the score, and no other notes or memories that you use to plan your practice. You decide tomorrow’s focus from those minute totals alone. In that case, where you got stuck has not entered the plan. This does not mean you practised carelessly. It means the record did not preserve the particular difference you now need to ask about.
Writing 40.0 minutes, or even recording the time to the second, will not recover the missing bar. What you need might be no more than a sentence: “Went wrong again where the left hand comes in.”

Of course, if your teacher already heard the mistake and used it to plan the next day’s practice, you cannot stare at the notebook and declare that nobody dealt with it. A small box failing to capture something does not mean the whole process failed to take it in.

sections.heading: 4. Some differences really don’t matter this time
paragraphs: Take another small example. A reading course uses a test to check whether applicants can keep up. Let’s make the conditions explicit: a score of eighty is enough, there are plenty of places, and everyone who reaches the threshold can enrol. Applicants who qualify are not ranked against one another.
One applicant scores ninety, another ninety-five. The person handling enrolment records only “qualifies” and does not retain the five-point difference.

Is something missing? Not for the admission task as we have defined it. Both applicants meet the stated condition, and those five points do not change what should happen when they enrol. The reason is not “They both got in anyway.” It is that we specified beforehand that this task was only to establish whether each applicant met the threshold.

Now change the task: select the applicant with the highest test score, with the selection rule explicitly based on scores. Those five points matter. Two entries saying “qualifies” cannot stand in for the order of the scores. This is a different task that needs to be checked afresh. We cannot simply carry over the previous finding that the record was adequate.

Not every arrangement in everyday life has to give a complete account of a person. An application form that does not record all your talents is not thereby denying that you have them. To ask whether it left something out, we need to ask whether that particular thing matters to the task at hand.
Respecting people’s worth also means not requiring every form to serve as a verdict on their entire life.

sections.heading: 5. A no is not the same as being ignored
paragraphs: Back to Lin. This is a different version of the situation: set aside what we established about the earlier process.

This time, the scheduler does read her availability. They confirm with her that a late shift would require other arrangements for picking up her child. They check everyone else’s hours and try several possible swaps. Those availability constraints are used to draw up the options; when suitable cover is available, her shift can be changed accordingly.

In the end, they still cannot move her off this Wednesday’s late shift. She may be disappointed. Whether the arrangement is fair, and whether the extra burden it places on her is reasonable, remain open questions.

But if that work really took place, an unchanged schedule is not enough to show that her situation was never considered. A factor can enter a decision without outweighing all the other factors every time. Two identical late shifts can be the end points of very different processes.

The reverse is true as well. Getting the result you wanted does not prove that your input was used. A system might happen to assign Lin an early shift without ever reading her comment. We are looking for the actual path in between, not just checking whether the destination suits her.

And “we took it into account” is not a certificate exempting management from criticism. A decision can genuinely consider your circumstances and still be deeply unfair. An omission, meanwhile, need not be addressed only by meeting every request in full. Whether something entered the process and how people ought to be treated are questions we need to discuss separately.

sections.heading: 6. “We don’t know yet” can be useful
paragraphs: Usually, we do not have all the information these examples give us. We have an automatic reply, a new schedule, or someone saying, “We considered everyone’s circumstances.”

At that point, do not turn suspicion straight into a finding. Ask: who looked at this field later? How was it used in scheduling? Was there a way to review the arrangement or swap shifts? Was that route actually used this time? A procedure’s existence on paper does not prove that anyone followed it. Not having seen it happen does not prove that nobody did.

Not every question can be answered immediately. Some records may still be unavailable. Some purposes may never have been made clear. Writing down what is missing is more useful than forcing the case into either “all sorted” or “completely ignored.”

Here we can introduce one slightly technical word: remainder. For the tool described in this essay, it means something specific that matters to the purpose of this particular task but has not been taken into account in actually carrying it out. It might be an availability constraint left out of scheduling, or the location of a mistake left out of a practice plan.
Remainder is not a label for Lin. We are checking whether one of her needs was taken into account, not calling the whole person something left over.

And the label can expire. Next month, the scheduler starts checking these constraints one by one and actually uses them in drawing up options. For that new round of scheduling, this particular item is no longer a remainder. Perhaps only the handover changed; not a single line of the form did. We should recognise that change, not keep insisting it was never handled just to make our original criticism eternally right.

sections.heading: 7. A small note is enough
paragraphs: Next time someone says, “We’ve recorded it,” you do not have to start by arguing about the entire institution. Take a piece of paper and write down a few specific things.
items: Which task are we talking about? Note its purpose, the people or things involved, the rules used to handle it, and the particular round or day you are checking.

Which difference am I asking about? For example, whether Lin can or cannot work on Wednesday evening. Don’t just write “my whole situation,” and don’t switch purposes mid-check to get the conclusion you want.

Why does this difference matter? If it were different, what would need to change in the arrangements for the same purpose? If it is irrelevant, its absence from the record is not grounds for calling it an omission.

Where did it go next? Find records, discussions, checks or reviews that were actually used. Check whether another route brought the information back into this particular process. Don’t rely only on whether the answer was yes or no.

What can we say so far? Where the evidence supports it, write “relevant, but not taken into the process,” “taken into the process,” or “not relevant to this task.” If you cannot decide yet, name the specific evidence still missing. New evidence may justify a different finding.
after: You do not need to find an omission just to fill the page. Confirming that this particular item was taken into account is a useful check too. And failing to identify another item to check does not prove that the whole arrangement is now free of problems.

Whether anything should change next, how to change it, and who should bear the cost all require further judgment. Finding a missing connection does not create time, staff or money. Nor does it automatically settle everyone’s priorities.

The point of this small note is to help the conversation move forward instead of going round in circles. Lin need not first prove that the whole shop is indifferent to people. The scheduler cannot answer her merely by handing back the file that has been safely archived. They can begin with one clear question: how, exactly, was her Wednesday availability used in this round of scheduling?
We’ve received your feedback. That can be the beginning of something. If there is a next step, the word “received” will not take it for us.

reading_note: This essay draws on Remainder: A Portable Method (M-00E). Its everyday situations are invented examples. Readers do not need to learn the dimension sequence or the full methodology first. The question here is whether specific, relevant content has entered a process in which it can actually affect how the matter is handled. We do not assume that every case must contain an omission, or infer a verdict of good or bad, a duty to act, or an inevitable next step merely from finding one. The paper gives fuller requirements for evidence, a record sheet and four supporting classifications. Those classifications are not an exhaustive list, and you do not need to memorise them to use this essay.
